source.title_on_document: FIERO: Empowering Creative Writing Through Collaborative Game Play

supplement.where: Appendices A?H, pp. 41?51 of this PDF. Appendix H, p. 51, points to https://github.com/zxioke/FAIero-game for system, card, and prompt artifacts.
supplement.holds: Appendix A, Tables 1?2 (pp. 41?42), contains self-report scale/item means, SDs, group counts, Mann?Whitney z statistics, p values, and effect sizes r. Appendix B gives interview questions; C provides participant demographics; D gives the story-evaluation prompt; E gives participant instructions; F gives models and prompts; G describes conflict resolution; H describes the artifact release. Output-comparison percentages and overall chi-squared tests are in the main text/Figures 13?14 (pp. 27?29). No additional participant- or team-level standard errors for those output outcomes are supplied in the appendices, and no separate statistical supplement is identified.

paper_design_summary: Sixty participants were randomly assigned to FIERO or Google Docs collaborative writing, then worked face to face in teams of three to create superhero stories; FIERO bundled physical cards with AI-generated images, decision support, and story refinement (pp. 12?16, ??3.4?4.4). Participants completed self-report questionnaires, and three LLM judges evaluated final stories on seven dimensions (pp. 14?17, ??4.2?4.5). The content analysis used nine texts per condition and repeated story-pair comparisons, despite ten teams per condition being reported (pp. 16?17, ??4.4 and 4.5.2).

studies.label: FIERO versus Google Docs: face-to-face collaborative superhero-story writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were assigned to story creation using Google Docs or card-game story creation using FIERO, then organized into three-person teams. Both conditions used the same face-to-face format, rounds, and task. FIERO varied physical cards, interface, AI images, and optional AI text assistance together (pp. 13?14, ?4.1). The paper states participant randomization but does not describe its implementation or how team formation related to allocation.
assignment.quote: In this between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to either a story creation group or a card game-based story creation group.
assignment.locator: p. 13, ?4.1, Study Design; pp. 13?14, condition descriptions

arms.name: FIERO (card-game collaborative writing)
arms.description: Face-to-face teams used FIERO, physical narrative cards, a synchronized writing interface, generated images, optional AI decision suggestions, and final-story assistance. The reported analyzed questionnaire count is 30; the paper reports ten teams of three (p. 14, ?4.1; p. 16, ?4.4; p. 41, Table 1).

arms.name: Control (Google Docs collaborative writing)
arms.description: Face-to-face teams co-wrote in one shared Google Docs page using the same narrative phases and timing, with discussion and text review but no FIERO cards or AI assistance. The reported analyzed questionnaire count is 30; the paper reports ten teams of three (pp. 13?14, ?4.1; p. 16, ?4.4; p. 41, Table 1).

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusion procedure or attrition count is stated. The analyzed count of 60 refers to the questionnaire sample: n = 30 per group in Tables 1?2 (pp. 41?42) and N = 60 in ?4.5.1 (p. 17). The output analysis instead describes nine texts per condition (p. 17, ?4.5.2), although recruitment reports ten teams per condition (p. 16, ?4.4). The paper does not explain this difference or explicitly state the number of people represented by the analyzed texts. No output-specific people count is inferred. Arm-level randomized counts are left null because the arm counts are reported as recruited/analyzed rather than separately enumerated at assignment.
participants.who: Non-professional creators interested in collaborative creative writing, recruited through word of mouth and social media, aged 18?28; the text reports 80% students and 20% non-students in fields including technology, design, media, marketing, and administration (p. 16, ?4.4).
participants.quote: We recruited 30 participants for each of the Control and FIERO groups (divided into 10 teams of 3 members each) to take part in an offline collaborative writing activity.
participants.locator: p. 13, ?4.1 (60 randomized); p. 16, ?4.4 (recruitment and population); p. 17, ??4.5.1?4.5.2 (analysis counts); pp. 41?44, Appendices A and C, Tables 1?4

ai_tool.name_model: FIERO: GPT-4 for text assistance and GPT-4o image model (gpt-4o-image) for images, as reported on p. 12, ?3.4, and p. 49, Table 5. Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2 are post-hoc judges, not participant assistance.
ai_tool.how_used: Integrated assistance combined image generation from cards and player-authored text, context-sensitive selection among players' villain/weapon drafts with explanations, and final narrative suggestions/polishing. AI was available during production of the final stories; participants could accept, change, or reject suggestions. This is a multi-function, structured tool rather than unrestricted chat (p. 12, ?3.3.3; pp. 47?50, Appendices E?F; p. 51, Appendix G).

task.description: Teams collaboratively wrote a complete superhero story. Participants first drafted heroes and their backgrounds, then villains and settings, then weapons, discussing and integrating the contributions into a final narrative. Both conditions worked face to face; FIERO added physical cards and AI-supported digital features (pp. 13?14, ?4.1).
task.duration: 30 minutes; three rounds, each with 5 minutes of individual thinking and 5 minutes of group discussion (p. 13, ?4.1).

outcomes.name: Story creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The Creativity dimension evaluates originality, innovative concepts, uniqueness, fresh perspectives, and imaginative content (pp. 15?16, ?4.2.2; p. 46, Appendix D). Figure 14 reports a net advantage for FIERO over Control for each judge. These are printed percentages, not standardized effect sizes; no dimension-specific test or interval is reported. Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2 separately compared each of nine FIERO texts with each of nine Control texts. Every pair was presented in AB and BA order; inconsistent decisions became draws. Evaluator models are variants of the same outcome, not separate studies. The reported 81 comparisons per judge count story pairs, not people. Methods: p. 17, ?4.5.2; p. 26, ?5.4; comparison denominator: p. 27, ?5.4.1. No participant- or team-level standard error is reported.

contrasts.reported: Creativity net advantage (FIERO over Control): Claude ?27.2%; Gemini 50.6%; GPT-5.2 ?7.4%. Gemini favors FIERO; Claude and GPT-5.2 favor Control.
contrasts.locator: p. 28, ?5.4.2, Creativity; p. 29, Figure 14, Creativity row and caption

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly states that 60 participants were randomly assigned to the two conditions (p. 13, ?4.1), with AI-assisted FIERO versus a no-AI Google Docs baseline during story production (pp. 12?14, ??3.3.3?4.1). It reports 60 people analyzed in the study's questionnaires, 30 per arm (p. 17, ?4.5.1; pp. 41?42, Tables 1?2). The final stories receive automated creativity and other quality judgments (pp. 15?17, ??4.2.2 and 4.5.2; pp. 27?29, ?5.4 and Figures 13?14), so eligibility does not rely on self-reports. Caveats: the output-specific people count is not explicitly stated; nine texts per arm are analyzed despite ten teams per arm being reported. AI is bundled with the game/cards/interface, so the contrast does not isolate AI's contribution (p. 34, ?6.6.1). Repeated story-pair statistics do not supply participant- or team-level precision for pooling.

one_line_finding: FIERO's bundled card-game/AI condition was preferred overall, but creativity judgments differed by evaluator: net advantages were ?27.2% for Claude, 50.6% for Gemini, and ?7.4% for GPT-5.2 (p. 29, Figure 14).
open_questions: Why does the content analysis use nine texts per condition (p. 17, ?4.5.2) when ten teams per condition are reported (p. 16, ?4.4)? Which texts were omitted, and how many people are represented in the scored output sample?
How was participant randomization implemented, and when were teams formed relative to allocation? The assignment claim is explicit, but those procedures are not described (pp. 13?14, ?4.1).

How are the overall comparison in Figure 13 and the Overall Preference row in Figure 14 related? The prompt has both Overall and Final_Winner fields (p. 47, Appendix D), but their mapping is unstated; the Claude summaries do not reconcile as the same win-minus-loss measure.

Are underlying story-level judgments and team identifiers available to estimate uncertainty accounting for repeated use of the same stories? The paper reports pairwise chi-squared tests without team-level uncertainty (pp. 17 and 27). Appendix H's release description lists system, cards, and prompts but does not explicitly identify participant data or scoring data (p. 51).
notes: Read the complete markdown, including references and Appendices A?H; checked coded facts and numbers against PDF text and the printed labels in Figures 13?14. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. Outcome inventory: the seven scored story dimensions are Creativity, Overall Preference, Plot Coherence, Development, Language Use, Anthropomorphism, and Character Fidelity (pp. 15?16 and 27?29). The overall win/loss/draw summary is retained, separately labelled, within the overall-quality outcome rather than counted again; the unresolved relationship to the Overall dimension is flagged. The three evaluator models are retained as variants of each outcome. No effects or counts were calculated. Self-report inventory, not included as eligible output outcomes: CSI total and engaging, inspiring, immersive, vividness, intuitive items; CSE total and idea fluency, idea development, novelty generation, original output, idea persuasion items; SSA total and plot logic/Cognitive Engagement, novelty and originality, collaborative synergy, narrative integration, agency items (pp. 14?15, ?4.2.1; pp. 20?22, Figures 7?10; pp. 41?42, Tables 1?2). In particular, the abstract's idea-fluency and novelty-generation claims refer to confidence questionnaires, not measured idea counts or independently scored novelty. Figure 6 and Figures 11?12 give qualitative/illustrative comparisons rather than additional quantitative creativity outcomes (pp. 19, 24, 26). No cross-person similarity/diversity score or post-AI unassisted task is reported; qualitative discussion of homogenization is not a measured diversity outcome (p. 20, ?5.1.2; pp. 13?17, task and measurement sections). The industry practitioner helped design the judging rubric, but humans did not score the final output judgments; these are automated_score outcomes, not expert_raters (p. 17, ?4.5.2; p. 35, ?6.6.8). Appendix G supplies design/grounding discussion, not a separate scored creativity study (pp. 50?51). No shared participant sample or preregistration is reported. Participant country is unstated and has not been inferred from affiliations or story examples. The code URL is printed on p. 12, footnote 11, and p. 51, Appendix H; no explicit participant-data URL is supplied.
